author: Living next to the Grump
title: Living next to the Grump
text:
What She Can’t Say

Sophie

Iwish I could pretend their words didn’t follow me. But they do.


William with his measured concern, Caroline with her silence that cut deeper than anything she said aloud.


They looked at me like I was something to endure, not someone to trust. Like I was already a problem, just waiting to happen. A stain on Ethan’s judgment. A threat to Mia’s fragile progress.


Part of me wants to leave just to avoid proving them right. To stop pretending this isn’t hard, that I’m not already in over my head.


But Mia… she needs me. And somewhere along the way, I started needing her too.


I kneel beside Mia on the living room floor, her tiny frame trembling as she clutches the sleeve of my shirt. She doesn't cry, not loudly, not anymore. But her silence is louder than any sob could ever be.


Her breathing is uneven, her body curled tight in that way she does when the world gets too big, too loud, too uncertain.


My heart aches as I watch her shrink into herself, her small fingers gripping me like I’m the only stable thing in the room.


Her knuckles are pale, her face blotchy from earlier tears, and her wide, glassy eyes refuse to meet mine. It’s like she’s folded herself into the smallest version possible, hoping the storm will pass if she just stays invisible long enough.


I shift closer and hum softly, the same song I always use. A slow, familiar tune that once made her smile during a hard morning. One note, then another, low and steady, meant more to ground me than to comfort her, but it starts to work.


Her body doesn’t relax completely, but her breath begins to even out in slow little bursts, like she's trying to match the rhythm of my voice.


She doesn't look at me.


I gently place her bunny next to her knee. She doesn’t grab it, just lets it sit there like a familiar presence she’s not ready to hold.


Ethan watches from the doorway. He doesn’t move. His hand is still on the suitcase handle, knuckles white. His eyes are fixed on us, on her. His jaw clenches once, then again, and when I glance up, our eyes meet.


He doesn’t say anything at first. Just looks at me like he wants to memorize this moment. Then, his voice, soft, tired, torn, finds me in the quiet.


“When I come back… will you still be here?”


My lips part, but I don’t answer.


Because I don’t know how. Because every part of me wants to say yes, but something deeper, the part still scarred from everything I lost, holds me back.


Words stick in my throat, thick with the weight of what this could mean if I stay. If I hope.


And then the door closes behind him.


The soft click echoes through the room like a shift I can’t name. Final, somehow. Heavy.


Mia’s breathing slows as I wrap my arms around her a little tighter than necessary. Her head rests against my chest, her fingers tangled in the hem of my shirt. Maybe it’s for her comfort. Or maybe it’s mine. Because in this moment, I’m not just holding her.


I’m holding on to something I’m terrified to lose.


—


Later that afternoon, the house settles into a hush. Miss Dana has taken Mia outside for a walk in the yard. I stay behind, needing a minute to collect myself.


I make tea I don’t drink.


Open cabinets I don’t need anything from.


Walk into rooms only to forget why.


Eventually, I end up at the kitchen table, my phone buzzing with a new email notification. I swipe the screen out of habit.


Just a few days ago, a similar message had arrived: from Willow Creek Academy. They’d heard about my time with Mia and offered me a chance to apply for a position in their early education program. I hadn’t told anyone. I hadn’t even opened the attachment.


Because even then, something about leaving didn’t sit right.


And now…


Subject: Teaching Opportunity at Oakridge Elementary


My heart skips.


Then races.


I click it open, blinking at the words.


We were recently informed by Little Acorns Preschool about your experience and interaction with Mia Ford. Your background as an early childhood teacher with knowledge in special education and your response during a recent classroom visit deeply impressed our staff. We would love to speak with you about an upcoming opening on our early childhood and special education team. Please consider submitting your application.


I read it again.


Then a third time.


They want me to apply.


Me.


I press a hand to my chest, suddenly breathless.


That’s Mia’s school. The school I was afraid would never let someone like me near a classroom again.


They heard about me.


And they still reached out.


I set the phone down slowly, like any sudden movement might break the moment.


A second chance.


My career. My identity. My purpose.


All the things I thought were lost in the smoke of what happened in New York.


I close my eyes.


And I’m there again, standing in that boardroom, voice cracking as I defended a child no one else seemed to see. The silence afterward. The cool, rehearsed words of the superintendent thanking me for my "passion" before the meeting ended and everything fell apart.


I was right.


And I still lost everything.


I blink the memory away and stand, phone forgotten for now. I walk through the house slowly, like I’m seeing it for the first time.


There’s Mia’s half-finished train set on the rug, her glittery crayons scattered across the coffee table. Miss Dana’s laughter floats through the back door, followed by a burst of giggles from Mia.


In the corner of the kitchen, Ethan’s coffee mug sits beside mine, both still bearing faint lipstick and coffee stains from earlier. I pick mine up and feel the warmth long since gone.


On the back of the couch, the scarf I wore two days ago is still draped, half-folded and slipping to the floor. No one moved it. No one cleaned it up.


Because this place… it doesn’t feel temporary anymore.


Not for me.


Not for the girl who once walked back into town with a suitcase full of doubts and no plan beyond survival.


This house, this life, feels like something I’ve unknowingly been building piece by piece. Like I’ve already started unpacking without realizing it.


I glance down the hallway and catch a glimpse of Mia spinning in slow circles with Miss Dana. Her cheeks are pink, her little feet bare. The sunlight catches her hair and turns it gold.


“Maybe this is something real…” I whisper.


And that thought alone terrifies me.


I turn away from the hallway and lean against the kitchen counter, staring at nothing.


What happens if I apply?


What happens if I get the job?


Can I still be here for Mia and Ethan if I step back into that world? What if the past follows me? What if I’m not ready?


What if I am?


I press a hand over my heart, trying to quiet the thrum beneath it. “Why now?” I whisper into the stillness.


Why now, when I’m finally starting to feel like I belong?


I don’t have an answer.


Only questions.


Only the slow ache of uncertainty settling in again, like it always does when something good finally starts to feel possible.


I close the phone screen. The email stays unread for the fourth time.


I stay standing in the kitchen.


Stuck between the woman I used to be… and the life that’s quietly growing in front of me.


—


I step out onto the porch as the sky shifts to dusky pink. The air is cool, brushing soft against my skin. I wrap my arms around myself, holding in whatever this feeling is. A pull between two versions of home—one built from the career I lost, and the other growing quietly around the people I never expected to love.


The porch boards creak softly beneath my feet, a grounding sound in the silence. The hum of crickets rises, steady and familiar, mixing with the distant sound of laughter from a house down the street. Someone’s baking, cinnamon maybe, and the scent drifts faintly through the breeze.


The stars are just starting to peek through the clouds. I tip my head back, searching for constellations I used to trace with my finger as a kid. Back when everything felt smaller and simpler.


For a long time, I just stand there.


Still.


Silent.


Trying to figure out if I’m brave enough to want more than what I came back for.


Trying to believe that maybe… I’m allowed to want this. To stay. To choose something soft and uncertain. To choose them.


Then, with a soft breath, I turn around and quietly step back inside.


The warmth of the house wraps around me, comforting and familiar. I walk through the kitchen and into the living room, where Miss Dana and Mia are sorting puzzle pieces on the floor.


I offer a small smile as I pass, and Dana gives me a nod of understanding before returning her focus to Mia.


I settle onto the armrest of the couch, trying to shake the weight in my chest.


Moments pass.


The murmur of Mia’s voice and Miss Dana’s soft encouragement fills the space like a gentle rhythm.


As I step through the threshold, I hear it.


Mia’s voice, small and tentative, drifting from the hallway.


“Will he come back?”


My hand freezes.


I don’t move.


I don’t breathe.


Then my voice, quiet and unsure, rises before I can stop it.


“I don’t know,” I whisper.


The air around me stills.


And just then, the front door creaks open.


I turn sharply.


My heart skips.
